'''Jeannette Elizabeth Brown''' (born May 13, 1934<ref>{{Cite web|title = Brown, Jeannette E. (Jeannette Elizabeth), 1934- - LC Linked Data Service (Library of Congress)|url = http://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/no2011075403.html|website = id.loc.gov|accessdate = 2015-11-13}}</ref>) is a retired American organic medicinal chemist, historian, and author.

==Life and education==
Brown was born in 1934 in [[The Bronx, New York]]. According to Brown, when she was young, she contracted tuberculosis, and was treated by Arthur Logan. Logan was a young African-American in his intern year of residency, and lived in Brown's building. Brown's later inspiration to study science came from asking Logan how one could become a doctor. He replied, "Oh, you study science".<ref name="acsblog" /> Brown excelled in particular in chemistry, scoring 98 out of 100 on the [[New York State Regents]] chemistry exam.<ref name="acsblog" /> She attended New Dorp High School on [[Staten Island]], and graduated in 1952.<ref name="acsblog">{{cite web|title=Making a Difference with Research: Profile of Jeannette Brown|url=https://communities.acs.org/community/society/industry-voices/blog/2015/02/27/making-a-difference-with-research-profile-of-jeannette-brown|website=American Chemical Society|accessdate=21 February 2016|date=27 Feb 2015}}</ref><ref name="hm">{{cite web|title=Jeannette Brown|url=http://www.thehistorymakers.com/biography/jeannette-brown-42|website=The HistoryMakers African American Oral History Video Collection|accessdate=21 February 2016}}</ref> Brown earned her [[bachelor's degree]] in chemistry at [[Hunter College]] in 1956, one of two African Americans in the inaugural class of Hunter's chemistry program.<ref name=Grezlla>{{cite news|last1=Grezlla|first1=Paul|title=Chemical reactions Hillsborough chemist shares pioneering stories of black women|url=http://www.mycentraljersey.com/article/20120305/NJCOLUMNIST/303050015/Chemical-reactions|accessdate=13 November 2015|work=My Central Jersey|date=March 16, 2012|archive-date=17 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117014329/http://www.mycentraljersey.com/article/20120305/NJCOLUMNIST/303050015/Chemical-reactions|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1958, she became the first African American woman to achieve a [[master's degree]] from the [[University of Minnesota]] in organic chemistry.<ref>{{cite web|title=Jeanette E. Brown, Chemist, Historian, and author of "African American Women Chemists," to Speak August 18|url=http://diversity.lbl.gov/2014/07/30/african-american-chemist-discusses-science-history-at-august-18-talk/|publisher=Berkeley Lab|date=30 July 2014|accessdate=13 November 2015|archive-date=17 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117031501/http://diversity.lbl.gov/2014/07/30/african-american-chemist-discusses-science-history-at-august-18-talk/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Her [[master's thesis]] was entitled "Study of Dye and Ylide Formation in Salts of 9-(p-dimethylaminophenyl) Fluorene."

==Chemical research==
After receiving her master's degree, Brown began work as a research chemist at [[Novartis#Ciba-Geigy|CIBA Pharmaceutical Company]], where she was involved in research programs for [[drug development]] targeting [[tuberculosis]] and [[coccidiosis]]. She moved to [[Merck & Co.|Merck]] in 1969, where she co-authored 15 publications, obtained one patent and contributed to five others. Brown's work focused on synthesizing novel medicinal compounds. She worked to develop the compound cilastatin sodium. Cilastatin is an inhibitor of renal dehydropeptidase. Since the antibiotic, imipenem, is one such antibiotic that is hydrolyzed by dehydropeptidase, cilastatin is used in combination with imipenem to prevent its metabolism.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cilastatin|url=https://www.drugbank.ca/drugs/DB01597|website=www.drugbank.ca|access-date=2020-04-24}}</ref> This combination creates the antibiotic [[Imipenem/cilastatin|Primaxin (imipenem/cilastatin)]], which is used to treat severe internal infections, as well as diseases caused by flesh-eating bacteria and some types of [[pneumonia]].

To succeed in industry, she believed that being an effective communicator, working on a team, and having a strong scientific education in an ever-changing field were essential.

== Outreach ==
Brown spent 36 years in research before she switched over to education. From 1993 to 2002 she was a visiting professor at the [[New Jersey Institute of Technology]],<ref name="hm" /><ref name="Grezlla" /> where she also helped recruit black students to enter [[STEM]] fields and worked on science education issues in the state. It was here that she also tutored middle school and high school chemistry teachers. She won a grant from the [[Camille and Henry Dreyfus Foundation]], which she put towards tutoring chemistry teachers. Brown has also devoted significant professional effort to diversity and outreach projects; she served on the [[National Science Foundation]] Committee on Equal Opportunities for Women Minorities and Persons with Disabilities and was the historian of the [[American Chemical Society]]'s Women Chemist Committee.<ref name="Grezlla" /> To this day, Brown continues to mentor both middle and high school students through the Freddie and Ada Brown Award. She founded this award in 2010 in honor of her parents.

== Work as historian ==
As a historian of science, Brown contributed seven biographical profiles of African American chemists to the [[African American National Biography Project]], which included the first African American women to get their Ph.Ds in chemistry and chemical engineering.<ref name="hm" /> She is the author of the 2011 book ''African American Women Chemists'', which profiles early African American women in chemistry.<ref name="neal2">{{cite journal|last1=Neal|first1=Sharon L.|date=2 April 2012|title=Black Women, Chemistry Pioneers|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/90/i14/Black-Women-Chemistry-Pioneers.html|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|volume=90|issue=14|pages=46–7}}</ref> Her second book, ''African American Women Chemists in the Modern Era'', focuses on contemporary women who have benefited from the [[Civil Rights Act]] and are now working as chemists or chemical engineers.

== Quotations ==
In an interview with the University of Minnesota, Brown advises young women entering the scientific fields to plow ahead despite the inevitable slights that will come their way. “You just got to keep going,” she said. “You can't stop. If you stop, you're not going to get what you want.”<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://cse.umn.edu/college/feature-stories/jeannette-brown-compounding-chemicals|title=Jeannette Brown: Compounding chemicals {{!}} College of Science and Engineering|website=cse.umn.edu|access-date=2019-03-08|archive-date=2021-11-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211122170216/https://cse.umn.edu/college/feature-stories/jeannette-brown-compounding-chemicals|url-status=dead}}</ref>

“Go straight for a Ph.D. Do not stop at a master's degree,” she said. “If you're a Ph.D., then you're the boss.”<ref name=":0" />

"I think working hard and learning new things keeps you young."<ref name="acsblog" />

==Awards and honors==
* 1991, elected to Hunter College Hall of Fame<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://chem.umn.edu/news/alumna-jeannette-brown-writes-new-book-african-american-women-chemists|title=Alumna Jeannette Brown writes new book on African American Women Chemists|last=Department of Chemistry|date=2018-07-12|website=University of Minnesota - College of Science and Engineering|language=en|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2020-03-06}}</ref>
*2004, [[Société de Chimie Industrielle (American Section)|Société de Chimie Industrielle]] Fellow of the Chemical Heritage Foundation (American Section)<ref name=":1" />
*2005, Outstanding Achievement Award<ref>[http://uawards.umn.edu/recipients-outstanding-achievement-award/jeanette-e-brown Outstanding Achievement Award]</ref> recipient, University of Minnesota
*2005, National Award for Encouraging Disadvantaged Students into Careers in the Chemical Sciences recipient, [[American Chemical Society]]<ref name=":1" />
*2007, [[Association for Women in Science]] fellow<ref name="hm" />
* 2009, Glenn E. & Barbara Hodson Ullyot Scholar of the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]]<ref name="neal2" />
* 2009, [[American Chemical Society]] fellow in the Division of Professional Relations<ref name="acsfellows">{{cite web|title=ACS Fellows|url=http://prof.sites.acs.org/acsfellows.htm|website=American Chemical Society|accessdate=21 February 2016|archive-date=5 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170405153530/http://prof.sites.acs.org/acsfellows.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2020, Henry Hill Award, American Chemical Society<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chem.umn.edu/news/alumna-jeannette-brown-receives-acs-henry-hill-award|title=Alumna Jeannette Brown receives ACS Henry Hill Award|last=harva015|date=2020-02-21|website=Department of Chemistry|language=en|access-date=2020-03-06}}</ref>
